intro: Every skater solves physics problems with their body. Standing on a narrow board, a rider keeps their center of mass over four small wheels. Leaning into a carve, they let the trucks steer and let friction pull them around a curve. Popping a 180, they twist against the ground and then ride the spin they carry into the air. Pumping a bowl, they gain speed without ever putting a foot down.

This unit names the ideas behind those moves: center of mass and base of support, the geometry of trucks, centripetal force, the limits of grip, speed wobble, torque, angular momentum and moment of inertia. You will work through real numbers in meters, seconds, kilograms and newtons, using g = 9.8 m/s². You will also learn how to set up trucks, calm a wobble, pump a bowl and practice a frontside 180 step by step, with safety first.

By the end you will be able to explain why a board turns when you lean, calculate the inward force a carve needs, predict how much faster a skater spins when they tuck, and show where the energy of a pump comes from.
bigQuestion: How do balance, turning and spinning on a skateboard follow the same laws of motion that govern every moving object?

test.q: A skater tips over when the line down from the center of mass:
choices: Falls outside the base of support
test.why: Gravity tips an object once its center of mass is no longer above its base of support.

The hangers swing on a slanted line and twist the axles
The bearings stop on one side
test.why: Truck geometry turns a tilt of the deck into a twist of the axles, which steers the board.

Tighter, so the board turns less
test.why: Loosening the nut lets the bushings relax, so a smaller lean turns the board.

test.why: A low stance with gentle front-foot pressure calms the wobble; sharp corrections and back-foot weight feed it.

Their moment of inertia is zero

Where does the extra energy of a faster spin come from when a skater tucks?

test.why: Backside means the back and heels face the obstacle.

title: Balance, Turning and Spin

chapters.title: Center of Mass and Turning
chapters.bigQuestion: How does a skater stay on top of a narrow board and make it curve just by leaning?

story.title: A Curve Drawn in Chalk Dust
story.kicker: A rider leans into a long carve, and the wheels leave a curve on the ground.
paragraphs: Late on a Saturday afternoon, Dana rolls across the empty lot behind the community center. The concrete is smooth and dry. Someone has drawn hopscotch squares in chalk near the fence, and a thin layer of chalk dust has blown across the ground.

Dana pushes twice with her back foot, then sets it on the tail. Her helmet is buckled, and her knee pads are snug. She bends her knees and lets her weight settle over her toes. The board begins to curve toward the toe side, slow and smooth, like a pencil drawing an arc.

She shifts her weight back onto her heels. The board swings the other way. Toe side, heel side, toe side again. She never steers with her hands or twists the board with her feet. She only leans, and the board answers.

When she rolls back over the chalk, she stops and looks down. Four wheels have left four thin lines in the dust. The lines are not straight. They form a long, wavy S that shows exactly where each lean began and ended.

Her friend Marcus walks over and points at the lines. "How does leaning make it turn?" he asks. "The board doesn't have a steering wheel." Dana laughs, picks up the board and flips it over to show him the trucks.
story.think: When you lean on a bike, a scooter or a skateboard, what do you think makes the path curve instead of making you fall over?

sections.title: Balance and the Center of Mass

lessons.title: Where Your Weight Is Centered
lessons.mainIdea: The center of mass is the single point where an object's weight acts as if it were all gathered together.
reading: Lay a ruler across one finger and slide it until it stays level. The spot where it balances is its *center of mass*, the point where the ruler's weight acts as if all of it were gathered in one place. For a plain ruler, that point is right in the middle. Gravity pulls on every bit of the ruler, but you can treat all those pulls as one pull on that single point.

A standing person has a center of mass too. For most people standing straight, it sits roughly at hip level, a little below the belly button, in the middle of the body. It is not fixed to one spot on your skin. When you raise your arms, it moves up a little. When you bend your knees and crouch, it drops lower. When you lean forward, it moves forward.

A skateboard has its own center of mass, usually close to the middle of the deck between the bolts. When you stand on the board, you and the board act together. Because a rider weighs many times more than a board, the combined center of mass is mostly set by where the rider's body is. Skaters control balance by moving their own center of mass with their knees, hips, arms and shoulders.

words.d: the point where an object's weight acts as if it were all gathered in one place
the pull of the Earth on every object, pulling it toward the ground
to bend the knees and hips so the body gets lower

look.title: Find the Balance Point
look.text: Hold a skateboard deck flat across one hand, trucks down. Slide your hand toward the nose and the tail tips down. Slide it toward the tail and the nose tips down. Somewhere near the middle, the board rests level. Now tape a small bag of coins near the nose and try again. The balance point has moved toward the nose.
look.prompt: Why does adding weight near the nose move the balance point toward the nose?

check.q: What happens to your center of mass when you bend your knees into a crouch?
choices: It moves to your feet exactly
check.why: Crouching brings the body closer to the ground, so the center of mass drops lower.

check.q: Where is the center of mass of a plain wooden ruler?
choices: At the heaviest end of any object
check.why: A plain ruler has its weight spread evenly, so it balances in the middle.

check.q: Why is the combined center of mass of a rider and board set mostly by the rider?
choices: The rider weighs many times more than the board
The board has no center of mass
The trucks cancel the board's weight
check.why: The rider is much heavier than the board, so the rider's position decides where the combined center of mass is.

lessons.title: The Base of Support
lessons.mainIdea: An object stays balanced while its center of mass is above its base of support.
reading: Stand with your feet together and have a friend give your shoulder a gentle nudge. You wobble. Now stand with your feet wide apart and try again. You barely move. The difference is your *base of support*, the area on the ground outlined by everything touching it. Wide feet make a wide base.

The rule of balance is simple to say. An object stays upright while a straight line down from its center of mass lands inside its base of support. If that line falls outside the base, gravity pulls the object over. A tall, narrow bookcase tips more easily than a short, wide one because a small lean moves its high center of mass past the edge of its narrow base.

A skateboard's base of support is the rectangle between the four spots where the wheels touch the ground. From nose to tail it is long, the length of the *wheelbase*, the distance between the front and back wheels. From toe side to heel side it is narrow, only as wide as the wheels are apart. That is why falling forward or backward off a rolling board is less common than tipping toward the toes or heels.

words.d: the area on the ground outlined by every point that touches it, such as feet or wheels
the distance between the front wheels and the back wheels of a board
keeping the center of mass above the base of support so you do not tip over

look.title: Two Bookcases
look.text: Picture two bookcases with the same weight. One is tall and thin. One is short and wide. Tilt each one a little to the side. The tall one's center of mass is high, so a small tilt carries it past the edge of its narrow bottom and it falls. The short one's center of mass is low and its bottom is wide, so it rocks back.
look.prompt: Which skater would you expect to be steadier: one standing straight with feet close together, or one with knees bent and feet over the bolts? Explain using base of support.

check.q: When does an object tip over?
choices: When its base of support is on the ground
When its center of mass is very low
When the line down from its center of mass falls outside its base
check.why: Gravity tips an object when the point below its center of mass is outside the base of support.

check.q: Which direction is a skateboard's base of support narrowest?
choices: From toe side to heel side
It is the same in every direction
check.why: The base is only as wide as the wheels are apart from toe side to heel side, but it is as long as the wheelbase from nose to tail.

check.q: What does the wheelbase measure?
choices: The distance between the front and back wheels
check.why: The wheelbase is the distance from the front wheels to the back wheels.

lessons.title: Staying Up on a Rolling Board
lessons.mainIdea: Bent knees lower the center of mass and let a rider make the small corrections that keep it over the board.
reading: Before rolling, practice balance standing still on grass or carpet so the board cannot roll away. Wear a helmet that fits and is buckled, and add wrist guards and pads while you learn. Put your front foot just behind the front bolts and your back foot over or just in front of the back bolts. Bend your knees as if you were about to sit on a high stool, and keep your shoulders lined up over the board.

Bent knees help in two ways. First, they lower your center of mass, so a small bump moves it a shorter distance sideways. Second, they work like springs. A straight-legged rider passes every jolt from a crack straight up into the hips. A rider with soft knees can absorb the jolt and keep the upper body still. Riders make many tiny corrections to keep the center of mass over the narrow base. Each *correction* is a small shift of weight through the ankles, hips or arms.

The same idea explains a *manual*, rolling on two wheels with the nose or tail up. In a back-wheel manual, the base of support shrinks from a rectangle to a thin line between the two back wheels. The rider must hold the center of mass right over that line. Too far back and the tail scrapes; too far forward and the nose drops. Practice manuals on carpet first, with a grown-up spotter if you are young.

words.d: a small shift of weight that moves the center of mass back over the base of support
rolling on only the back wheels or only the front wheels, with the other end lifted
the screws that hold the trucks to the deck; their spots on top are a guide for foot position

look.title: Balance Check on the Grass
look.text: Set the board on thick grass. Step on with the front foot behind the front bolts, then place the back foot over the back bolts. Bend both knees. Lean gently toward your toes, then toward your heels, and feel the board tilt under you. Now stand straight-legged and try the same small leans. Most people feel steadier with the knees bent.
look.prompt: Try this standing beside the board in your mind: why would a crack in the ground bother a straight-legged rider more than a rider with bent knees?

check.q: In a back-wheel manual, what shape does the base of support become?
choices: A thin line between the back wheels
check.why: With only the back wheels down, the base shrinks to the line between those two wheels.

check.q: Where should the front foot go when you first stand on the board?
choices: On the tip of the tail
On top of the back bolts
check.why: The front foot goes just behind the front bolts, and the back foot goes over or just in front of the back bolts.

check.q: Why do bent knees help a rider stay balanced?
choices: They lower the center of mass and absorb jolts
They make the wheels grip harder
They stop the trucks from turning
check.why: Bent knees lower the center of mass and act like springs that soak up bumps.

lessons.title: The Parts of a Truck
lessons.mainIdea: A truck is a set of metal parts held together by a kingpin, with rubbery bushings that let it tilt and spring back.
reading: Flip a skateboard over and look at one of the two *trucks*, the metal assemblies that hold the wheels. The flat part screwed to the deck is the baseplate. The T-shaped part that holds the axle is the *hanger*. The axle runs through the hanger and sticks out each side, and a wheel slides onto each end with two bearings inside it.

A thick bolt called the *kingpin* rises out of the baseplate and passes through the hanger. Around the kingpin, above and below the hanger, sit two rubbery rings called *bushings*. They are usually made of urethane, the same family of material as the wheels. A nut on top of the kingpin squeezes the bushings. The bushings hold the hanger in place but let it tilt, then push it back to center.

The hanger also has a short arm, the pivot, that pokes into a small cup in the baseplate. The pivot and the kingpin together set the line the hanger swings around. That line is tilted at an angle, not flat and not straight up. Because of that slant, tilting the deck makes the hanger turn, which is the secret of steering a skateboard by leaning.

words.d: the metal parts under the deck that hold the wheels and let the board turn
the T-shaped part of a truck that holds the axle and the wheels
the large bolt that holds a truck together and passes through the bushings and hanger
rubbery rings around the kingpin that let the hanger tilt and then push it back to center

look.title: A Truck Taken Apart
look.text: Picture a truck laid out on a towel, top to bottom: the kingpin nut, a cupped washer, the top bushing, the hanger with its axle, the bottom bushing, another washer, and the baseplate with the kingpin standing up from it. The hanger sits sandwiched between the two bushings like the filling between two slices of bread.
look.prompt: If the bushings were made of hard metal instead of rubbery urethane, what would happen when the rider leaned?

check.q: Which part of a truck holds the axle?
check.why: The T-shaped hanger holds the axle, and the wheels go on the axle's ends.

check.q: What do the bushings do?
choices: Let the hanger tilt and push it back to center
Hold the bearings inside the wheels
check.why: The rubbery bushings allow the hanger to tilt, then spring it back to the middle.

check.q: What passes through the bushings and the hanger?
check.why: The kingpin is the large bolt that rises from the baseplate through the bushings and hanger.

lessons.title: Leaning Turns the Wheels
lessons.mainIdea: Because the hanger swings on a slanted line, tilting the deck turns the axles, and the board curves toward the side you lean.
reading: Stand on a board on carpet and press down with your toes. The deck tilts toward the toe side. Underneath, each hanger swings on its slanted pivot line. A swing on a slanted line does two things at once: it lets the deck tilt, and it twists the axle so it no longer points straight across. The wheels now point a little to one side, the way the front wheels of a car point when the steering wheel is turned.

The front and back trucks face opposite ways, with their kingpins pointing toward each other. So when the deck tilts, the front axle and the back axle twist in opposite directions. Seen from above, the two axles are no longer parallel. Lines drawn out along the two axles would meet at a point off to one side of the board. That point is the center of the circle the board will roll around.

The result is easy to remember. Lean toward your toes and the board turns toward your toe side. Lean toward your heels and it turns toward your heel side. The harder you lean, the more the axles twist and the tighter the circle. This is called *carving* when you ride long, smooth arcs by leaning instead of lifting the front wheels. The *turning radius* is the radius of the circle the board traces.

words.d: riding long, smooth curves by leaning the board instead of lifting it
the radius of the circle a board traces as it turns; smaller means a tighter turn
the metal rod through the hanger that the wheels spin on

look.title: Two Axles Seen From Above
look.text: Imagine looking straight down through a clear deck while the rider leans toward the toes. The front axle twists so its toe-side end swings back. The back axle twists so its toe-side end swings forward. Draw a long line out from each axle on the toe side. The two lines cross a few meters away. The board rolls in a circle around that crossing point.
look.prompt: If the rider leans harder, do the axle lines cross closer to the board or farther away? What does that mean for the turn?

check.q: A rider presses down with the toes. Which way does the board turn?
check.why: Leaning toward the toes tilts the deck and twists the axles so the board curves toward the toe side.

check.q: Why do the front and back axles twist in opposite directions when the deck tilts?
choices: The trucks face opposite ways, kingpins toward each other
The back truck has no bushings
Only the front truck can move
check.why: The two trucks are mounted facing each other, so the same tilt swings their axles opposite ways.

check.q: What happens to the turning radius when a rider leans harder?
choices: It gets smaller, so the turn is tighter
check.why: A harder lean twists the axles more, so the circle gets smaller and the turn is tighter.

lessons.title: Tight Trucks and Loose Trucks
lessons.mainIdea: Tightening the kingpin nut or using harder bushings makes a board steadier but slower to turn; loosening does the opposite.
reading: Turning the kingpin nut with a skate tool changes how the board rides. Turning it clockwise squeezes the bushings, so the board has *tight trucks*: the hanger needs more lean to tilt, and the board resists turning. Turning it counterclockwise lets the bushings relax, so the board has *loose trucks*: a small lean makes a sharp turn.

Each choice has a cost. Tight trucks feel steady at speed and are less likely to shake, but they make sharp turns harder. Loose trucks carve tight circles and feel lively, but they react to every small wobble of the rider's ankles. Many riders adjust a quarter turn at a time, ride for a while, and adjust again. Bushings also come in different hardness, measured on a durometer scale like wheels. Softer bushings turn easier; harder ones feel steadier.

Keep the nut threaded far enough onto the kingpin that its locking ring grips the threads. A nut backed off too far can loosen on its own while you ride. Check both trucks after adjusting one, since uneven trucks make the board pull to one side. If the board turns too sharply while you are still learning to roll, tighten the trucks a little before you change anything else.

words.d: trucks with the kingpin nut turned down so the bushings are squeezed; steadier, slower to turn
trucks with the bushings less squeezed; quick, sharp turning but less steady
a scale that measures how hard a rubbery material is, used for wheels and bushings

look.title: Same Rider, Two Setups
look.text: A rider rides the same board twice down a gentle, empty path. First with tight trucks: the board holds a straight line, and the rider has to lean hard to curve around a cone. Then with loose trucks: the slightest lean sends the board curving, and the cone is easy to go around, but the board drifts whenever the rider's weight shifts.
look.prompt: A friend wants to carve around cones in an empty, closed lot. Another wants to roll straight and steady on a long path. Which setup would you suggest for each, and why?

check.q: What happens when you turn the kingpin nut clockwise?
choices: The bushings relax and the board turns more easily
The bushings are squeezed and the trucks get tighter
check.why: Turning the nut clockwise squeezes the bushings, which makes the trucks tighter.

check.q: Which is a trade-off of loose trucks?
choices: They turn sharply but react to every small wobble
check.why: Loose trucks turn easily but are less steady because small weight shifts steer the board.

check.q: Why should the kingpin nut stay far enough down on the threads?
choices: So its locking ring grips and it does not loosen while riding
check.why: The nut's locking ring has to grip the threads, or the nut can work loose during a ride.

lessons.title: Why a Turn Needs a Force
lessons.mainIdea: A moving object goes straight unless a force pushes it sideways; in a turn, friction from the ground pushes the board toward the center of the curve.
reading: Roll a marble across a smooth floor and it keeps going in a straight line until something stops it or pushes it aside. This is *inertia*, the tendency of a moving object to keep moving at the same speed in the same direction. Isaac Newton put it at the center of his first law of motion in 1687. A skater rolling across flat concrete would also go straight forever if no force acted.

To travel in a curve, an object needs a force that keeps pulling it toward the inside of the curve. This inward force is called *centripetal force*, which means center-seeking. Swing a ball on a string in a circle and the string is that force: it pulls the ball toward your hand. Let go of the string and the ball flies off in a straight line, not outward in a curve.

On a skateboard, nothing pulls on a string. The inward force comes from *friction* between the wheels and the ground. When the axles twist, the wheels try to roll in a curve, and the ground grips the urethane and pushes the wheels sideways toward the center of the circle. Even at a steady speed, a turning board keeps changing its direction of motion, so physicists say it is accelerating.

words.d: the tendency of an object to keep doing what it is doing: staying still, or moving straight at the same speed
the inward force that keeps an object moving in a curve, pointing toward the center of the circle
a force between two surfaces that resists sliding; it lets wheels grip the ground

look.title: Newton's First Law
look.text: Every body continues in its state of rest, or of moving uniformly in a straight line, unless it is forced to change that state by forces acting on it.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia, 1687; wording adapted from Andrew Motte's English translation, 1729
look.prompt: Use this law to explain why a skater who hits a patch of loose sand in the middle of a turn may slide off in a straight line.

check.q: On a turning skateboard, what supplies the centripetal force?
choices: Friction between the wheels and the ground
check.why: The ground grips the wheels and pushes them sideways toward the center of the curve.

check.q: What does centripetal mean?
check.why: Centripetal means center-seeking; the force points toward the center of the circle.

check.q: You swing a ball on a string and let go. Which way does the ball go?
check.why: With no inward pull, inertia carries the ball in a straight line.

lessons.title: Leaning Into the Carve
lessons.mainIdea: In a turn the rider leans toward the center so the ground's push stays in line with the center of mass; faster or tighter turns need more lean.
reading: Watch a rider carve and you will see the whole body tilt toward the inside of the turn. This lean is not just style. The ground pushes up on the wheels and also sideways, toward the center of the turn. If the rider stood straight up, that sideways push at the feet would tip them toward the outside, the way a rug pulled from under your feet tips you over. Leaning lines up the ground's total push with the rider's center of mass.

The needed inward *acceleration* depends on speed and radius: a = v² ÷ r, where v is speed in meters per second and r is the turning radius in meters. Worked example: a rider rolls at 5 m/s around a curve with a 5 m radius. Then a = 5² ÷ 5 = 25 ÷ 5 = 5 m/s². If the rider and board together have a *mass* of 60 kg, the inward force is F = ma = 60 × 5 = 300 N.

Compare that with the rider's weight: W = mg = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N. The sideways force is about half the weight, since 300 ÷ 588 ≈ 0.51. A rider leaning at about 27 degrees from straight up keeps the push balanced in this turn. The lean depends only on speed and radius, not on mass, so a light rider and a heavy rider carving the same line at the same speed lean the same amount.

words.d: a change in speed or direction each second, measured in meters per second squared (m/s²)
how much matter an object has, measured in kilograms
the unit of force; one newton gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s²

look.title: Inward Force on a 60 kg Rider, 5 m Radius
look.cite: Worked example: F = m × v² ÷ r with m = 60 kg and r = 5 m
look.prompt: Compare the force at 3 m/s and at 6 m/s. When the speed doubles, how many times bigger does the force get?

check.q: A rider goes 4 m/s around a curve with a 2 m radius. What is the inward acceleration?
Why does a rider lean toward the inside of a turn?
choices: To line up the ground's push with the center of mass
check.why: Leaning keeps the ground's combined push in line with the center of mass so the rider does not tip outward.

check.q: What is the weight of a 60 kg rider?
check.why: Weight is W = mg = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N.

lessons.title: Speed, Radius and Grip
lessons.mainIdea: Friction can only push so hard; if a turn needs more inward force than the wheels can grip, the board slides.
reading: The formula a = v² ÷ r has a surprise inside it. Because speed is squared, doubling the speed makes the needed inward force four times as large. Going three times faster needs nine times the force. Cutting the radius in half doubles the force. A turn that feels easy at a slow roll can be impossible at a fast one.

Friction has a limit. The most sideways grip the wheels can give is roughly μ × N, where N is the *normal force* pressing the wheels into the ground and μ (the Greek letter mu) is the *coefficient of friction*, a number that describes how grippy two surfaces are together. On level ground N equals the weight, so the largest possible turning acceleration is about μ × g. For example, if μ were about 0.7, the limit would be about 0.7 × 9.8 ≈ 6.9 m/s².

In that example, a rider at 8 m/s on a 5 m radius would need 8² ÷ 5 = 64 ÷ 5 = 12.8 m/s², almost twice the limit, so the wheels would slip. Skaters who want that slide do it on purpose in a powerslide, turning the board sideways to scrub off speed. Softer wheels usually grip rough ground better, and hard wheels slide more easily on smooth concrete. Sand, water and leaves lower μ a lot, which is why a wet or dusty turn can send a board out from under a rider.

words.d: the push of a surface straight out against whatever presses on it; on level ground it equals the weight
a number, written μ, that describes how strongly two surfaces grip; bigger means more grip
turning the board sideways on purpose so the wheels slide and the rider slows down

look.title: Turning Acceleration at Different Speeds, 5 m Radius
look.cite: Worked example: a = v² ÷ r with r = 5 m
look.prompt: If the grip limit were about 6.9 m/s², at which speeds in the chart could the wheels hold the turn?

check.q: If a rider doubles her speed through the same curve, the needed inward force becomes:
check.why: Speed is squared in a = v² ÷ r, so twice the speed needs 2² = 4 times the force.

check.q: On level ground, what is the largest possible turning acceleration before the wheels slide?
check.why: The grip limit is μN, and on level ground N = mg, so the limit on acceleration is μg.

check.q: Why can a sandy patch make a board slide out in a turn?
choices: It makes the turning radius larger
It lowers the coefficient of friction
check.why: Sand lowers μ, so the wheels cannot give as much sideways grip as the turn needs.

lessons.title: What Speed Wobble Is
lessons.mainIdea: Speed wobble is a fast side-to-side shaking that feeds on itself, most often at higher speeds with loose trucks or stiff legs.
reading: A rider is rolling faster than usual down a gentle slope in an empty lot. The board starts to shimmy: the trucks twitch left and right, a little at first, then harder and faster. Riders call this *speed wobble*. It can grow in a second or two from a buzz in the feet to a shake strong enough to throw the rider off.

Speed wobble is an *oscillation*, a motion that swings back and forth over and over. On a skateboard it can feed on itself. A tiny tilt steers the trucks, the turn tips the rider the other way, the rider corrects, and the correction overshoots into a tilt the other way. At higher speeds each swing happens faster than the rider can react smoothly, so the corrections arrive late and make the next swing bigger.

Several things make wobble more likely. Loose trucks or soft bushings let a small lean turn the wheels a lot. Stiff, straight legs pass every twitch through the body instead of soaking it up. Weight drifting onto the back foot is a common trigger, because it lets the front of the board wander. Going faster than you have practiced is the biggest factor of all. Wobble is not a sign that someone is a poor skater; experienced riders feel it too.

words.d: a fast side-to-side shaking of the board and trucks that tends to grow at higher speeds
a motion that swings back and forth over and over, like a swing or a plucked string
to push too far when fixing a lean, so you tip the other way

look.title: A Shopping Cart Wheel
look.text: Picture a shopping cart with one front wheel that flutters back and forth when you push it fast. Push slowly and the wheel rolls straight. Push faster and the flutter starts, then gets louder. Slow down and it calms. A skateboard in speed wobble is a bigger version of that flutter, with the rider's own reactions adding to the swing.
look.prompt: In the cart and the skateboard, what one change makes the flutter calm down? Why might that be?

check.q: What is an oscillation?
choices: A motion that swings back and forth over and over
A straight line at steady speed
check.why: An oscillation is a repeating back-and-forth motion, like a swing.

check.q: Which setup makes speed wobble more likely?
choices: Loose trucks and stiff, straight legs
Weight centered over the front foot
check.why: Loose trucks let small leans steer a lot, and stiff legs pass every twitch through the body.

check.q: Why does wobble grow at higher speeds?
choices: Each swing comes faster than the rider can smoothly react
check.why: At speed the swings come quickly, so late corrections overshoot and make the next swing bigger.

lessons.title: Calming a Wobble
lessons.mainIdea: To calm speed wobble, crouch lower, press gently on the front foot, relax and look ahead; prevent it by riding within your skill and setting trucks a little tighter.
reading: When the board starts to shake, the first move is to get low. Bend your knees and drop your hips so your center of mass sits closer to the board. A lower body swings less, and bent legs soak up the twitching. Next, move your weight forward so you press gently on your front foot. Pressure on the front truck helps hold it steady and keeps the front of the board from wandering. Then relax your ankles and look far ahead, not down at your feet.

Fighting the board with sharp, quick corrections usually makes wobble worse, because each sudden push becomes the next swing. Smooth, small pressure works better. If the shaking keeps growing and you are moving slowly enough, step off and run it out. If not, bail low: crouch, aim for the grass if it is close, and fall onto your pads and roll instead of reaching out with straight, locked arms.

Prevention is the best fix. Learn speed a little at a time on flat ground and gentle, empty slopes. Never ride hills that have cars, and never hold onto a moving vehicle. Tighten loose trucks a quarter turn, or try harder bushings, before riding faster. Wear a helmet that fits and is buckled, plus wrist guards and pads, every time you practice speed. Fear when the board shakes is a normal, useful signal that it is time to slow down.

words.d: how a rider stands on the board: where the feet go and how low the body is
to leave the board on purpose to avoid a worse fall
the foot nearer the nose of the board; for regular riders it is the left, for goofy riders the right

look.title: Wobble Response, Step by Step
look.text: The board starts to buzz under your feet. Step 1: bend your knees and sink your hips. Step 2: shift your weight forward and press gently through your front foot. Step 3: loosen your ankles and breathe out. Step 4: look far ahead down your path. Step 5: if it still grows and you are slow enough, step off and run; if not, crouch and fall onto your pads.
look.prompt: Practice steps 1 to 4 standing on the board on carpet. Which step changes how steady you feel the most?

check.q: When speed wobble starts, which foot should you press gently with?
choices: The back foot, hard on the tail
The back foot, on the heel side
check.why: Gentle pressure on the front foot helps hold the front truck steady.

check.q: Why do sharp, quick corrections usually make wobble worse?
choices: Each sudden push becomes the next swing
They lower the center of mass
check.why: Sudden pushes overshoot and feed the back-and-forth motion.

check.q: Which change helps prevent speed wobble?
choices: Tightening the trucks a little and building speed slowly
check.why: Slightly tighter trucks and gradual speed practice make wobble less likely.

review.q: A skater stays balanced as long as the line down from the center of mass falls:
review.why: Balance means the center of mass stays above the base of support.

review.q: Which part of the truck is squeezed when you tighten the kingpin nut?
review.why: The kingpin nut presses on the bushings; squeezing them makes the trucks tighter.

review.q: A rider leans toward the heels. What does the board do?
review.why: Leaning tilts the deck, the axles twist, and the board curves toward the side of the lean.

review.q: A 50 kg rider turns at 4 m/s on a 4 m radius. What inward force is needed?

choices: The tendency to keep moving straight at the same speed
review.why: Inertia is an object's tendency to keep doing what it is doing unless a force acts.

review.q: Why does the board slide out in a turn that is too fast or too tight?
choices: The bushings get softer at speed
The turn needs more inward force than friction can give
The center of mass rises to the deck
review.why: Friction has a limit of about μN; a turn that needs more than that makes the wheels slip.

review.q: Which stance helps calm a speed wobble?
choices: Low, knees bent, weight gently forward
review.why: A low stance with weight on the front foot steadies the board.

review.q: Why is a skateboard easier to tip toward the toes or heels than forward or backward?
choices: The nose is heavier than the tail
The deck is wider than it is long
The base of support is narrow from side to side but long from nose to tail
review.why: The wheels are close together side to side but far apart nose to tail, so the side-to-side base is narrow.

chapters.title: Rotation and Angular Momentum
chapters.bigQuestion: Once a skater leaves the ground, what decides how fast and how far they can spin?

story.title: The Spinning Stool
story.kicker: A skater on a lab stool pulls in her arms and spins faster without anyone pushing.
paragraphs: The physics room smells like dry-erase markers. In the middle of the floor sits a round lab stool that turns freely on its base. Ms. Ortiz holds up two plastic water bottles, each filled to the top. "Who wants to spin?" she asks. Jaylen, who skates the park after school every day, raises his hand first.

He sits on the stool and holds a bottle in each hand with his arms stretched straight out to the sides. Ms. Ortiz gives the stool a gentle push and steps back. Jaylen turns slowly, like a ceiling fan on its lowest setting. The class counts the turns out loud.

"Now pull them in," she says. Jaylen bends his elbows and hugs the bottles to his chest. The stool whips around so fast the class gasps. Nobody touched him. He pushes his arms back out, and the stool slows down again, as if someone had stepped on a brake.

Jaylen plants his feet to stop and laughs. "That's what happens on a 360," he says. "If I keep my arms out, I can't get all the way around. If I tuck them, the board comes around on its own." Ms. Ortiz writes two words on the board: angular momentum.
story.think: Nobody pushed Jaylen a second time. Where do you think the extra speed came from when he pulled his arms in?

lessons.title: Spinning Things Keep Spinning
lessons.mainIdea: Angular momentum, the amount of spin an object carries, stays the same unless an outside torque changes it.
reading: Spin a top on a smooth table and it keeps turning for a long time. It slows only because the table rubs its point and the air drags on it. Just as a rolling object tends to keep rolling straight, a spinning object tends to keep spinning. Physicists measure the amount of spin an object carries as its *angular momentum*.

Angular momentum depends on two things. One is how fast the object turns, called its *angular velocity*, often counted in rotations per second. The other is how its mass is spread out around the line it spins on, the *axis of rotation*. Written as a formula, L = Iω, where L is angular momentum, I is the moment of inertia (the spread of mass) and ω, the Greek letter omega, is the angular velocity.

The key rule is *conservation of angular momentum*: if no outside twist acts on an object, its angular momentum stays exactly the same. A skater in the air is a clear case. The air pushes back only a little, and nothing else can twist the skater, so the spin they carry when their wheels leave the ground is the spin they have until they land. They can change how it is shared out, but not the total.

words.d: the amount of spin an object carries; it equals moment of inertia times angular velocity (L = Iω)
how fast something turns, such as rotations per second
the imaginary line an object spins around
the rule that total angular momentum stays the same unless an outside torque acts

look.title: Spin in the Air
look.text: Picture a skater rolling up a low bank and lifting off for a small 180. As the wheels leave the bank, the skater is already turning. In the air, there is no ground to push against, so nothing outside can add spin or take it away. The skater and board turn together until the wheels touch down, and then the ground's friction stops the spin.
look.prompt: Why can't a skater who leaves the ground with no spin at all start a 180 once they are in the air?

check.q: In the formula L = Iω, what does ω stand for?
check.why: ω (omega) is the angular velocity, how fast the object turns.

check.q: When does an object's angular momentum stay the same?
choices: When it is on the ground
When no outside torque acts on it
check.why: Conservation of angular momentum holds when no outside twist acts.

check.q: What is the axis of rotation?
choices: The imaginary line an object spins around
The fastest part of a wheel
The bolt that holds the trucks
check.why: The axis of rotation is the line the object turns around.

lessons.title: Torque Starts and Stops a Spin
lessons.mainIdea: A torque is a twist; it equals the force times the lever arm, and it is the only thing that changes angular momentum.
reading: Push on a door near its handle and it swings open easily. Push with the same force right next to the hinges and it barely moves. The difference is *torque*, the twisting effect of a force. Torque equals the force times the *lever arm*, the distance from the pivot to where the force is applied, measured straight across. The unit is the newton-meter (N·m).

Worked example: you push on a door with a force of 20 N. At the handle, 0.8 m from the hinges, the torque is 20 × 0.8 = 16 N·m. Near the hinges, 0.1 m away, the torque is 20 × 0.1 = 2 N·m. The same push gives eight times the twist at the handle, because 16 ÷ 2 = 8. A longer lever arm means more turning effect from the same force.

A skateboard is full of lever arms. In a kickturn, the back foot presses on the tail, and the back wheels are the pivot. The tail sticks out past the back wheels, so a press on its end has a lever arm that lifts the nose. To spin the whole body, a skater needs torque from the ground through their feet. Friction between the shoes, the grip tape and the wheels on the ground lets the feet twist the board and body before takeoff.

words.d: the twisting effect of a force; torque equals force times lever arm
the distance from a pivot to the line where a force pushes
the point or line something turns around
the unit of torque: one newton of force on a one-meter lever arm

look.title: Torque From a 20 N Push at Different Distances
look.cite: Worked example: torque = force × lever arm with F = 20 N
look.prompt: What happens to the torque each time the lever arm doubles?

check.q: A skater presses with 300 N on the tail, 0.15 m behind the back axle. What is the torque about the axle?
check.why: Torque = force × lever arm = 300 × 0.15 = 45 N·m.

check.q: Why does a door open more easily when you push at the handle?
choices: The longer lever arm gives more torque
Friction is lower at the handle
check.why: The handle is far from the hinges, so the same force makes a larger torque.

check.q: Where does a skater get the torque to start a spin?
choices: From the air once they are flying
From the ground, through their feet, before takeoff
check.why: Twisting against the ground through the feet supplies the torque; the air cannot.

lessons.title: Winding Up for a 180
lessons.mainIdea: Skaters wind their shoulders the opposite way, then unwind as they pop, so the ground gives them spin before they leave it.
reading: Watch a skater set up a 180 and you will see a small move before the pop. Their shoulders and arms turn a little the opposite way, like a baseball batter pulling the bat back. This is the *wind-up*. A skater about to spin toward the front, for example, first turns the shoulders slightly toward the back.

The wind-up gives the skater a longer time and a bigger turn to work with. As they crouch and pop, they swing the shoulders hard in the spin direction. Their feet are still pressing on the board, and the wheels are still on the ground, so the twist of the upper body pushes against the ground through the legs. The ground pushes back with friction, and that outside torque gives the whole skater angular momentum just before takeoff.

Once the skater is in the air, the wind-up rule changes. Now the total spin is fixed. If the shoulders keep turning one way, the hips and legs swing slightly the other way to balance it. That is why skaters lead with the shoulders, let the hips follow, and let the board follow the hips. This *counter-rotation*, twisting the upper body one way so the lower body turns the other, is how a skater lines up the board in the air without changing the total spin.

words.d: turning the shoulders and arms a little the opposite way before spinning
twisting one part of the body one way so another part turns the opposite way
the snap of the tail against the ground that sends the board up in an ollie

look.title: The Batter and the Skater
look.text: A batter pulls the bat back over the shoulder, steps, and swings, with the feet pushing on the ground the whole time. A skater crouches, turns the shoulders slightly backward, then snaps them around as the tail pops. In both, the big twist happens while the feet still press on the ground, and the turning motion keeps going after the push ends.
look.prompt: Stand on carpet with no board. Jump and try to turn 180 degrees with no wind-up, then try with one. What changes?

check.q: Why must the shoulders swing while the wheels are still on the ground?
choices: So the ground can supply the outside torque for the spin
check.why: The ground's friction provides the torque only while the skater is still touching it.

check.q: In the air, the shoulders keep turning one way. What do the hips and legs do?
check.why: Total spin is fixed in the air, so turning the upper body one way swings the lower body the other way.

check.q: In what order do the body and board turn in a 180?
check.why: Skaters lead with the shoulders, the hips follow, and the board follows the hips.

lessons.title: The Stool Experiment
lessons.mainIdea: Pulling the arms in lowers the moment of inertia, so the spin speeds up to keep angular momentum the same.
reading: Jaylen's stool spin is a classic physics demonstration. With his arms out, his mass is spread far from the axis of rotation. With his arms in, more of his mass sits close to the axis. Nothing outside twists him either way. Since his angular momentum L = Iω cannot change, a smaller I has to go with a larger ω.

Worked example with made-up but realistic numbers: suppose Jaylen and the stool have a moment of inertia of 3.0 kg·m² with his arms out, and he turns at 1 rotation per second. His angular momentum is 3.0 × 1 = 3.0 units. He pulls in, and his moment of inertia drops to 1.5 kg·m². Then 1.5 × ω = 3.0, so ω = 3.0 ÷ 1.5 = 2 rotations per second. Halving I doubles the spin rate.

Skaters use this every time they spin. In a 360 on a ramp or a big spin in the air, a skater who tucks the arms close and keeps the knees bent turns faster with the same takeoff. Reaching the arms out works the other way: it slows the spin. That is useful near the landing. Skaters often *spot* the landing, turning the head to look at it, and open the arms a little to slow down and settle before the wheels touch.

words.d: how hard it is to change an object's spin; it is larger when mass is spread far from the axis
one full turn of 360 degrees around an axis
to look at the landing during a spin so you know where you will come down

look.title: Same Angular Momentum, Different Arm Positions
look.cite: Worked example: L = Iω held at 3.0 kg·m² × 1 rotation per second
look.prompt: Check one row yourself: multiply the moment of inertia by the spin rate. What do you get every time?

check.q: A skater's moment of inertia drops from 2.4 to 1.2 kg·m² in the air. If they started at 1 rotation per second, how fast do they spin now?
check.why: L stays 2.4 × 1 = 2.4, so ω = 2.4 ÷ 1.2 = 2 rotations per second.

check.q: Why does pulling the arms in make a skater spin faster?
choices: It lowers the moment of inertia while angular momentum stays the same
It adds torque from the air
check.why: With L fixed, a smaller I means a larger ω.

check.q: Why might a skater open the arms a little near the landing?
choices: To slow the spin and settle
check.why: Spreading the arms raises the moment of inertia, which slows the spin.

lessons.title: How Mass Spread Out Matters
lessons.mainIdea: Moment of inertia grows with the square of distance from the axis, so mass far out counts much more than mass close in.
reading: For a small heavy object turning around an axis, the moment of inertia is I = m × r², where m is the mass in kilograms and r is the distance from the axis in meters. The unit is kilogram meter squared (kg·m²). The square matters a great deal. Moving a weight twice as far out makes its moment of inertia four times as large.

Worked example: hold a 2 kg dumbbell 0.2 m from your body's axis. Its moment of inertia is 2 × 0.2² = 2 × 0.04 = 0.08 kg·m². Stretch your arm so it is 0.8 m out. Now I = 2 × 0.8² = 2 × 0.64 = 1.28 kg·m². Moving it four times as far out made it sixteen times harder to spin, because 1.28 ÷ 0.08 = 16. A whole body is many small pieces added up the same way.

This explains how skaters shape their spins. In a tight tuck, arms, knees and head stay close to the axis, so the moment of inertia is small and the body turns quickly. A skater stretched out straight, arms wide, has a large moment of inertia and turns slowly. The board counts too. A deck held flat under the feet near the axis adds little, but a board flung out to the side adds a lot.

words.d: the unit of moment of inertia, written kg·m²
a body position with knees and arms pulled in close to the middle
a number multiplied by itself, such as 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64

look.title: A 2 kg Weight at Different Distances
look.cite: Worked example: I = m × r² with m = 2 kg
look.prompt: From 0.2 m to 0.4 m, the distance doubles. How many times bigger does the moment of inertia get?

check.q: What is the moment of inertia of a 3 kg weight held 0.5 m from the axis?
A weight is moved twice as far from the axis. Its moment of inertia becomes:
check.why: I depends on r², and 2² = 4.

check.q: Which body position has the smallest moment of inertia?
check.why: A tuck keeps the body's mass close to the axis, so I is smallest.

lessons.title: Where the Extra Spin Energy Comes From
lessons.mainIdea: A faster spin has more motion energy, and that energy comes from the muscles doing work to pull the arms in.
reading: If angular momentum stays the same, where does the extra speed come from? The answer is *rotational kinetic energy*, the motion energy of a spin. It equals ½ × I × ω², with ω measured in radians per second. A *radian* is a way of measuring angle; one full rotation is 2π radians, about 6.28 radians.

Worked example using the stool numbers: 1 rotation per second is about 6.28 radians per second. With the arms out, the energy is ½ × 3.0 × 6.28² = 1.5 × 39.4 ≈ 59 J. With the arms in, the spin is 2 rotations per second, about 12.57 radians per second. Now the energy is ½ × 1.5 × 12.57² = 0.75 × 158 ≈ 118 J. The spin energy doubled, from about 59 J to about 118 J.

The extra energy came from Jaylen's arms. Pulling heavy bottles inward while spinning takes effort, because the bottles tend to fly outward in a straight line. His muscles did *work*, which is force applied over a distance, and that work became spin energy. When he reached back out, the energy went the other way. A skater who tucks hard in the air is doing the same work with arms, legs and core.

words.d: the motion energy of a spinning object, equal to ½ × I × ω²
a unit of angle; one full turn is 2π radians, about 6.28
energy moved by a force pushing or pulling something over a distance; measured in joules

look.title: Feel the Pull
look.text: On a spinning stool with a grown-up spotting, hold a full water bottle in each hand, arms out. As you turn, you can feel the bottles tugging outward. Now pull them in toward your chest. Your arms have to work to bring them in, and the stool speeds up. Push them back out slowly and feel the stool slow down as the bottles move away.
look.prompt: Angular momentum stayed the same, but energy did not. In your own words, what is the difference between the two?

check.q: About how many radians are in one full rotation?
check.why: One rotation is 2π radians, about 6.28.

check.q: When the stool rider pulls the arms in, what happens to the rotational kinetic energy in the example?
choices: It doubles, from about 59 J to about 118 J
check.why: With I halved and ω doubled, ½Iω² goes from about 59 J to about 118 J.

check.q: Where does the extra spin energy come from?
choices: Work done by the rider's muscles pulling the arms in
check.why: The muscles do work pulling the weights inward, and that work becomes spin energy.

lessons.title: How to Pump
lessons.mainIdea: To pump, crouch as you ride into each curve of the bowl, then push up to stand tall as you pass through the curve.
reading: A *bowl* is a skatepark pool with curved walls all around. A rider can gain speed in it without ever pushing with a foot. The trick is *pumping*: crouching and standing at the right moments. Before you try, you should already roll comfortably on flat ground and ride up and down a small *transition*, the curved part where a wall meets the floor. Wear a helmet that is buckled, plus knee pads, elbow pads and wrist guards, and start in a small, shallow bowl when it is not crowded.

First, roll across the bottom with your knees bent and your weight centered between the bolts. Next, as you ride down a wall toward the curve, sink low into a crouch. Then, as the board passes through the curve and you feel your feet pressed harder into the deck, push up through both legs and stand tall, like a jump that never leaves the board. Ride up the next wall a little, crouch again as you come back down, and push again through the curve.

It feels like a rhythm: low, push, low, push. Common problems have simple fixes. If you push too early, on the flat, you gain almost nothing, so wait until you feel the curve press into your feet. If you lean back on the way up a wall, your board can shoot out in front of you; keep your shoulders over your feet. If you do fall, try to land on your knee pads and slide down the wall instead of putting out straight arms.

words.d: a skatepark pool with curved walls on every side
crouching and then standing up at the right moments to gain speed on curved walls without pushing
the curved part of a ramp or bowl where the floor bends up into the wall

look.title: One Pump, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: roll across the flat bottom with knees bent. Step 2: ride down the wall and sink into a crouch as the floor starts to curve. Step 3: feel the curve press the deck into your feet. Step 4: push up through both legs and stand tall through the curve. Step 5: sink again as you come back down the next wall. Repeat.
look.prompt: Act out the five steps on carpet without a board, saying low and push out loud. Where in the rhythm does the push happen?

check.q: When should a rider push up and stand tall while pumping?
choices: As the board passes through the curve
At the very top of the wall
check.why: The push works best in the curve, where the deck presses hardest into the feet.

check.q: What is a transition?
choices: The curved part where the floor bends into the wall
A change from regular to goofy
check.why: A transition is the curve between the floor and the wall.

check.q: What is a safe way to fall in a bowl?
choices: Land on your knee pads and slide down the wall
Catch yourself with straight, locked arms
check.why: Sliding on knee pads spreads the fall out; locked arms can hurt the wrists.

lessons.title: Why Pumping Adds Speed
lessons.mainIdea: Standing up where the curve pushes hardest lets the legs do more work than crouching gives back, and the extra becomes speed.
reading: In a curve, the deck must push the rider toward the center of the curve, not just hold them up. So the push on the feet is larger than the rider's weight. Worked example: a 60 kg rider moves at 5 m/s through a curve with a 2 m radius. The extra inward acceleration is v² ÷ r = 25 ÷ 2 = 12.5 m/s². At the bottom of the curve the deck pushes with about 60 × (9.8 + 12.5) = 60 × 22.3 ≈ 1,338 N. On the flat it pushes only 60 × 9.8 = 588 N.

Standing up means pushing against that force over a distance, and work equals force times distance. Raising the body 0.3 m in the curve takes about 1,338 × 0.3 ≈ 401 J of work. Crouching again on a wall or the flat, where the push is near 588 N, gives back only about 588 × 0.3 ≈ 176 J. The difference, about 401 − 176 = 225 J, stays in the motion as extra *kinetic energy*.

Check the gain: at 5 m/s the rider's kinetic energy is ½ × 60 × 5² = 750 J. Adding 225 J gives 975 J, so the new speed is √(2 × 975 ÷ 60) = √32.5 ≈ 5.7 m/s. Angular momentum gives a second view of the same idea. In the curve, the rider circles around the curve's center, and standing up moves their mass closer to that center, like Jaylen pulling his arms in. A child on a playground swing pumps in a similar way.

words.d: the energy of motion, equal to ½ × mass × speed²
the unit of energy and work; one newton pushing over one meter is one joule
how heavy you feel, which is the push of the surface under you; it grows in a curve

look.title: Push on a 60 kg Rider's Feet
look.cite: Worked example: push = m × (g + v² ÷ r) with m = 60 kg and g = 9.8 m/s²
look.prompt: Why does pumping work better when the rider is already moving fast through the curve?

check.q: Why is the push on a rider's feet bigger in the curve than on the flat?
choices: The deck must also push the rider toward the center of the curve
Gravity is stronger in a bowl
check.why: In a curve the deck supplies the inward centripetal push on top of holding up the rider's weight.

check.q: In the example, about how much energy does one pump add?
check.why: Standing in the curve takes about 401 J, crouching gives back about 176 J, and 401 − 176 ≈ 225 J.

check.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 60 kg rider at 4 m/s?

lessons.title: What Frontside and Backside Mean
lessons.mainIdea: Frontside means your chest and toes face the wall or the direction of a spin; backside means your back and heels face it.
reading: Skaters describe direction by which side of the body faces something, not by left or right. When you ride up to a wall or a ledge with your chest and toes facing it, you are riding *frontside*. When your back and heels face it, you are riding *backside*. This works the same for regular riders, who stand with the left foot forward, and goofy riders, who stand with the right foot forward.

Spins use the same idea. In a frontside spin, the skater turns so the chest swings around toward the direction of travel, and during a frontside 180 the skater faces forward halfway through. In a backside spin, the back turns toward the direction of travel first, so halfway through a backside 180 the skater's back faces where they are headed. Because the words describe the body, a regular and a goofy rider doing a frontside 180 actually turn in opposite directions as seen from above.

These words also name grinds, slides and airs. A frontside grind on a curb means you approach with the curb on your toe side. A backside grind means the curb is on your heel side. After a 180, the skater rolls *fakie*: in their normal stance, but moving backward with the tail in front. Learning both directions balances the body and gives a skater more ways to ride a park.

words.d: facing the wall, obstacle or direction of a spin with your chest and toes
facing the wall, obstacle or direction of a spin with your back and heels

look.title: Two Riders, One Curb
look.text: A regular rider and a goofy rider roll side by side toward the same curb, both facing it with their chests and toes. Both are riding frontside. Now they turn around and roll back the other way with the curb behind their heels. Both are riding backside, even though their feet point opposite ways.
look.prompt: Stand in your stance on carpet. Which way would you turn to face forward halfway through a 180? Is that frontside or backside?

check.q: A skater rolls toward a ledge with the ledge on the heel side. How is the skater riding?
check.why: Backside means the back and heels face the obstacle.

check.q: What does riding fakie mean?
choices: Riding with the opposite foot forward
Riding in your normal stance but rolling backward
check.why: Fakie is your normal stance, moving tail first.

check.q: Halfway through a frontside 180, which way is the skater facing?
choices: Forward, toward the direction of travel
Backward, away from the direction of travel
check.why: In a frontside spin, the chest swings toward the direction of travel.

lessons.title: The Frontside 180 Ollie
lessons.mainIdea: A frontside 180 ollie is an ollie with a wind-up: shoulders turn first, the hips follow, and the board lands rolling fakie.
reading: Learn this only after your ollie is steady and you can roll fakie comfortably. Practice on smooth, flat, empty ground in a helmet and pads. A good first step is the frontside kickturn 180: while rolling slowly, press the tail, lift the front wheels, and pivot all the way around on the back wheels, turning your chest toward the direction you are going. This teaches the shoulder-first turn with the wheels still near the ground.

For the ollie version, set your feet as for an ollie: the ball of your back foot on the tail and your front foot just behind the front bolts. First, crouch and wind your shoulders slightly backside. Next, pop the tail with your back foot and, at the same moment, swing your shoulders frontside and slide your front foot up toward the nose. Then let your hips follow your shoulders and guide the board around with both feet. Finally, land with both feet over the bolts, knees bent, rolling fakie.

Two problems are common. If the board turns only about 90 degrees, your shoulders probably stopped early; wind up a little more and turn your head to spot the landing over your front shoulder. If you land with one foot off the board, your front foot may have dragged too far; level the board by pressing evenly with both feet in the air. Start with a small pop. Height can come later, once the turn feels smooth.

words.d: pressing the tail to lift the front wheels and pivoting on the back wheels
a jump where the back foot pops the tail and the front foot slides up to level the board in the air
the foot nearer the tail of the board

look.title: Frontside 180, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: roll slowly in ollie position. Step 2: crouch and turn your shoulders slightly backside. Step 3: pop the tail with your back foot. Step 4: swing your shoulders frontside as your front foot slides up. Step 5: let your hips and the board follow. Step 6: spot the ground and land on the bolts, knees bent. Step 7: roll away fakie.
look.prompt: Which steps happen while the wheels still touch the ground, and why does that matter for the spin?

check.q: What should a skater practice before the frontside 180 ollie?
choices: A frontside kickturn 180 on flat ground
A drop-in on a tall ramp
check.why: The frontside kickturn 180 teaches the shoulder-first turn with the wheels near the ground.

check.q: In a frontside 180 ollie, which foot pops the tail?
check.why: The back foot pops the tail while the front foot slides up toward the nose.

check.q: The board turns only about 90 degrees. What is the likely fix?
choices: Wind up more and spot the landing over your front shoulder
Loosen the trucks all the way
check.why: A short turn usually means the shoulders stopped early; more wind-up and turning the head helps.

lessons.title: Practicing Spins Safely
lessons.mainIdea: Spins are learned in small steps: quarter turns, then half turns, low and slow, with a plan for falling.
reading: Every big spin is built from small ones. Many skaters start with tic-tac style quarter turns, lifting the front wheels and pivoting about 90 degrees on the back wheels while standing still on carpet. Next they try a full 180 kickturn standing still, then rolling slowly. Only after that do they add a small pop. Each step should feel calm before the next one begins. Fear is a normal signal that a step is too big; break it into a smaller piece.

Spinning in both directions matters. Most skaters find one direction easier at first. Practicing backside 180s as well as frontside 180s balances the body and teaches the brain to spot the landing from both shoulders. A backside 180 uses the same physics: wind the shoulders frontside, pop, then swing the shoulders backside so your back turns toward the direction of travel.

Falling small is part of every spin practice. If a landing goes wrong, step off the board toward the side it is not rolling, bend your knees, and let your body crouch. If you are going down, aim to land on pads and roll onto the side of your body, keeping your arms bent rather than locked straight. Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries, and wrist guards help prevent them, which is why they belong on every spin session.

words.d: learning a skill in small steps, each a little harder than the last
a half turn in which the skater's back turns toward the direction of travel first
pads with stiff splints that protect the wrists in a fall

look.title: Protecting Wrists
look.text: Skaters should wear a helmet, wrist guards, elbow pads and knee pads. Wrist guards help protect against wrist injuries, which are common when skaters fall onto their hands.
look.cite: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, skateboarding safety guidance
look.prompt: Why might wrists get hurt so often in skateboard falls? What habit protects them besides wearing guards?

check.q: What is the best first step toward learning a 180 spin?
choices: Small quarter-turn pivots standing still on carpet
A 180 off a set of stairs
check.why: Progression starts with small pivots while standing still before adding rolling and pop.

check.q: In a backside 180, which way do the shoulders swing after the pop?
check.why: The skater winds frontside first, then swings the shoulders backside after the pop.

check.q: Why do wrist guards belong on every spin session?
choices: They raise the moment of inertia
Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries
They keep shoes on the board

review.q: What does angular momentum depend on?
choices: Only the speed of the wheels
Moment of inertia and angular velocity
review.why: L = Iω, the moment of inertia times the angular velocity.

review.q: A 25 N push is applied 0.4 m from a pivot. What is the torque?
Why do skaters wind up their shoulders before a 180?
choices: To get spin from the ground before takeoff
review.why: Swinging the shoulders while the feet press the board lets the ground provide the torque for the spin.

review.q: A skater in the air pulls in arms and knees. What happens?
choices: The skater gains angular momentum from the air
review.why: A smaller moment of inertia with the same angular momentum means a faster spin.

review.q: Moment of inertia is larger when:
choices: Mass is close to the axis
Mass is spread far from the axis
The object is on the ground
review.why: I = m × r², so mass farther from the axis counts much more.

review.q: While pumping a bowl, when does the rider crouch?
choices: Only at the very end of the session
While riding down a wall toward the next curve
review.why: The rider sinks low coming down the wall, then stands tall through the curve.

review.q: A goofy rider's chest and toes face a ledge. How is the rider riding?
review.why: Frontside means chest and toes face the obstacle, for goofy and regular riders alike.

review.q: After a frontside 180 ollie, the skater rolls away:
choices: Switch, with the opposite foot forward
review.why: A 180 reverses the board, so the skater rolls backward in their normal stance, which is fakie.
